# Pyrolysis-Ultrasonic-Assisted Flotation Technology for Recovering Graphite and LiCoO from Spent Lithium-Ion Batteries

Guangwen Zhang,† Yaqun He,\*,†,‡ Yi Feng,† Haifeng Wang,† and Xiangnan Zhu§

ABSTRACT: An environmentally-friendly technology of pyrolysis-ultrasonic-assisted flotation for recovering graphite and LiCoO from spent lithium-ion batteries has been evaluated in this paper. Surface properties and morphology of graphite and LiCoO derived from spent lithium-ion batteries were carefully studied, and on this basis, their pyrolysis characteristics were investigated by thermogravimetry−gas chromatography−mass spectroscopy. Advanced analysis techniques, scanning electron microscopy, X-ray fluorescence spectrometry, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, were utilized to analyze the effect of pyrolysis and ultrasound on the surface properties and morphology of graphite and LiCoO2. Flotation tests were conducted to

evaluate the reinforcing effect of pyrolysis−ultrasound on flotation behavior. Results show that organic binder and electrolyte are the main reasons that graphite and LiCoO2 are hard to separate by flotation; meanwhile, pyrolysis can effectively decompose organic binders at a pyrolysis temperature of 500 ^∘C, and ultrasonic cleaning can effectively remove residual pyrolysis products. Pyrolysis-ultrasonic-assisted flotation can make the LiCoO2 grade improve from 67.25% to 93.89% with the recovery improving from 74.62% to 96.88%. This research work may provide an alternative process for the preparation of high purity L̅ ̅i̅ ̅C̅ ̅o̅ ̅O̅2̅ ̅^̅-̅ particles for the subsequent chemical metallurgy.

KEYWORDS: Spent lithium-ion battery, Recycling, Electrode materials, Pyrolysis-ultrasonic flotation

## ■ INTRODUCTION

Since lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) are the important link between sustainable energy and people’s daily life, they have been extensively used in various electronics, such as cameras, mobile phones, laptop computers, etc., because of their high energy density, low self-discharge, long storage life, and safe handling.1 With the rapid development of new-energy vehicles, large amounts of LIBs will play more important roles in energy storage and conversion. However, the average lifetime of LIBs is 2−3 years; this means that the expanding demand for LIBs will produce a large quantity of spent LIBs in the next few years.2 These spent LIBs contain valuable materials including metallic shell, anode, cathode, membrane separator, and other hazardous materials such as electrolyte. Cathodes are mainly composed of aluminum foil and cathode materials, i.e., LiCoO2, LiMn2O4, and LiFePO4, as well as other lithium metal oxides while anode contains copper foil and graphite.3 Therefore, it is a significant process for disposal of spent LIBs from the viewpoint of recourse recycling and environmental protection.

Because of the high content of valuable metals, especially for Co, Li, Mn, Ni, and Cu, recycling spent LIBs has attracted more and more attention. Researchers have proposed many sophisticated technologies to recycle spent LIBs. Hydro metallurgy processes play an important role in the recycling process of valuable metals released from spent LIBs, and it accounts for approximately 52% of the total recycling technologies.4 Furthermore, the main processes of hydrometallurgy comprise chemical leaching,5 exchange,9 chemical deposition,10 and electrochemistry,11 as well as mechanochemistry.12,13 In addition, pyrometallurgy is another effective technology for recycling valuable metals from spent LIBs.14,15 However, previous hydrometallurgy and pyrometallurgy technologies always focus on high-economic value metals recovery from cathode materials because of their high cost and potential secondary pollution. How to obtain cathode materials with high purity is the core process that determines the hydrometallurgy efficiency. Now, the spent LIBs are first dismantled, and then, cathodes are collected to be as objective in the current hydrometallurgy process. The manual dismantling process makes large-scale industrialization dificult because of economic and health perspectives. It is urgent to develop a pretreatment technology of spent LIBs to obtain high purity cathode materials for the hydrometallurgy process.

Recently, physical processes have been proposed to pretreat spent LIBs to obtain high purity cathode materials, which can provide raw materials for the hydrometallurgy technologies. Physical processes consist of discharging, crushing, sieving, and separation.16−18 The spent LIBs were fully discharged, and the impact crusher was utilized to break up the spent LIBs and detach the components. The crushed products were sieved to obtain a fine electrode mixture. The high-efficient flotation technology has been proved to realize the separation between cathode and anode materials because of their obvious hydrophilic/hydrophobic difference caused by different crystal texture.19,20 By this flowchart, the high purity cathode materials were obtained. However, electrode particles from the mechanical crushing process are enveloped by organic binder and residual organic electrolyte, which results in their original surfaces not being exposed, and the flotation process cannot realize the efficient separation of cathode and anode materials because of the same hydrophilicity and hydrophobicity. Removal of organic binders and electrolyte from cathode and anode particles will determine the flotation efficiency. Removal of organic binders and electrolyte using Fenton solution has been reported by He et al.21 However, the addition of Fe2+ in Fenton solution will remain in electrode particles, which make the subsequent chemical purification complex.22 Roasting technology has been used to remove organic binders and electrolyte, but secondary pollution will be produced in the combustion process.23,24 High flotation efficiency has been obtained, but it should not be recommended. Pyrolysis is a useful method to recover organic materials, and it has been used in recycling of waste printed circuit boards and waste plastics.25,26 Pyrolysis also has been studied to make electrode materials detach from copper/aluminum foils by Sun and Qiu.27,28 They found that pyrolysis is an efficient method to remove organic binders from electrode materials. Pyrolysis is used to remove organic binders and electrolyte, it not only can remove the organic binder but also can recycle organics. Ultrasonic technology has been utilized to clean a particle’s fl 29,30 Therefore, pyrolysis-ultrasonic pretreatment may remove organic binder and electrolyte on the surface of electrode particles and enhance their flotation process.

In this paper, a novel method of pyrolysis-ultrasonic-assisted flotation was proposed to recycle graphite and LiCoO from spent LIBs. Pyrolysis characteristics of electrode materials were analyzed by thermogravimetry−gas chromatography−mass spectroscopy (TG-GC/MS). Advanced analysis technologies of scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray fluorescence spectrometry (XRF), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) were used to obtain the morphology, chemical composition, and chemical states of surface elements of electrode material particles before and after pyrolysis. On the basis of these analyses, the nonfloatability mechanism of electrode materials was analyzed. The effect of pyrolysis on the surface chemical properties and floatability of electrode materials was investigated. Pyrolysis-ultrasonic-assisted flota tion experiments were conducted to evaluate the separation behavior of electrode materials.

## ■ EXPERIMENTAL SECTION

Sample Preparation. Spent LIBs from waste mobile phones were collected and pretreated following the procedure shown in Figure 1. They were first discharged with 5 wt % NaCl solution for 48 h and then naturally air-dried. To obtain pure cathode and anode materials, a manual dismantling process instead of mechanical crushing was conducted, and then, the cathode and anode were obtained from this process, respectively. Electrode materials were obtained by combining the crushing and sieving process. In order to prevent the overcrushing of aluminum and copper foils, the crushing time is controlled at 25 s. Previous studies have demonstrated that electrode materials are mainly concentrated in fine size fraction. Therefore, the 0.075 mm size screen hole was used to obtain electrode materials with fine size in this study. Three kinds of samples were prepared including cathode materials (LiCoO ), anode materials (graphite), and an electrode material mixture (LiCoO and graphite). As a result, the cathode material and anode material are obtained to, respectively, analyze their physicochemical properties and pyrolysis characteristics. Electrode material mixtures will be processed by pyrolysis or pyrolysis− ultrasound and then used for flotation.

Sample Pyrolysis Procedures. First, pyrolysis characteristics of cathode and anode materials were, respectively, analyzed by TG-GC/ MS which included a thermogravimetric analyzer (TGA) (Labsys Evo1600, France), auto injector system (Automation Autoinjector Corp., Italy), and GC/MS (TRACE GC Ultra/ISQ Single Quadrupole MS, USA). TG tests were first conducted to analyze the decomposition process of organics in raw LiCoO and graphite particles, and then, pyrolysis products at weight loss temperature were collected and injected into the GC/MS system by an auto injector system. Pyrolysis experiments of electrode material mixtures were conducted in a controlled atmosphere tube furnace (MXG1200-80, Shanghai Micro-X furnace Co., Ltd.). In each experiment, the 5 g sample was placed into the corundum tube and the tube was sealed by flanges at both ends. A vacuum pump was first applied to provide the vacuum environment, and then, the corundum tube was filled with high purity nitrogen with the gas flow of 200 mL/min. Gas pyrolysis products could be taken out of the tube by nitrogen flow, and then, macromolecular organics could be collected by condensation while small molecule organic gases were treated by a gas-treating system. Pyrolysis temperature increased from an initial temperature of ∴ _ 30 to a terminal temperature of 500 ^∘C at a heating rate of 10 ^∘C / m i n. Samples would be processed at an isothermal temperature of 500 °C for 30 min. Afterward, the samples were naturally cooled to 30 ^∘C in a nitrogen atmosphere. After pyrolysis, a part of the pyrolytic electrode material was treated by ultrasound at solid/liquid ratio of 1:10 g/mL with an ultrasonic frequency of 25 kHz and electric power of 800 W for 2 h. Afterward, electrode materials were separated by the filtration method and dried at 80 ^∘C. By these processes, three samples were prepared for flotation: raw electrode material mixture (REM), pyrolytic electrode material mixture (PEM), and pyrolysis-ultrasonic pretreated electrode material mixture (PUEM).

Flotation Procedures. Three kinds of flotation feeds (REM, PEM, PUEM) were utilized in the flotation process. LiCoO is hydrophilic due to the polarity ionic crystal whereas anode material graphite is hydrophobic due to its nonpolarity. Thus, graphite will attach to the bubble’s surface and then is recovered from the top foam layer, while LiCoO2 is collected in the tailings in the flotation process. Flotation experiments were conducted using an XFD-63 flotation machine at pulp density of 40 g / L,, impeller speed of 1800 rpm, and aeration quantity of 2.0 L/min, and the flow sheet of the flotation is shown in Figure 2. n-Dodecane and methyl isobutyl carbinol (MIBC)

were used as collector and frother, and their dosages were 300 and 150 g / t, respectively. LiCoO2 concentrate and graphite concentrate were obtained by filtration and drying, and then, their compositions were obtained from XRF analysis.

Measurement Methods. The TG-GC/MS was used to analyze the pyrolysis products. An XPS (ESCALAB 250Xi, America) at room temperature in an ultrahigh vacuum (UHV) system was used to analyze the chemical states of surface elements. By XPS analysis, element content on the surface of the electrode particles could be obtained to present the nonfloatability of electrode materials. The morphology of the electrode material particles before and after pyrolysis was determined using an SEM (FEI quanta 250, United States). Chemical components of electrode materials, LiCoO concentrate, and graphite concentrate were analyzed by XRF (Bruker S8 Tiger, Germany).

## ■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Pyrolysis Characteristics of Electrode Materials. Pyrolysis characteristics of raw LiCoO and graphite derived from spent LIBs are analyzed by TG-GC/MS. The TG results are shown in Figure 3, and pyrolysis products at pyrolysis temperatures of 120 and 500 ^∘ that correspond to the weight loss peaks in the DTG curve are present in Figure 4. The first weight loss stage appears when pyrolysis temperature ranges from 30 to 150 ^∘C; this is mainly caused by the volatilization of residual electrolyte. The decomposition of organic binder causes the second weight loss during the temperature of 450 to 550 ^∘C.. Similar TG and DTG curves of LiCoO2 and graphite demonstrate that the LiCoO2 and graphite used in this study have the same organic binder of PVDF. The DTG analysis shows the maximum weight loss appears at 500 ^∘C, and it indicates that pyrolysis can make organic binders fully decompose at 500 ^∘Ċ. Therefore, the pyrolysis experiments are conducted at a temperature of 500 ^∘C

On the basis of the TG analysis, the pyrolysis products of electrode materials at temperatures of 120 and 500 ^∘C were sampled via the auto injector system that was connected with the GC and TGA system, and gas analysis was conducted in the GC/MS system. Figure 4 demonstrates that pyrolysis products at a pyrolysis temperature of 120 ^∘C come from ester electrolyte, such as dimethyl carbonate, ethylene carbonate, and propylene carbonate. Organic pyrolysis products at a pyrolysis temperature of 500 ^∘C are mostly fluorides that mainly come from the decomposition of PVDF, such as vinylidene fluoride, 1,3,5-trifluorobenzene, 1,4-difluoroben zene, ^1, 1, 1, 3, 3, 3 -hexafluoro-propane, and 1,2,4-trifluoroben zene, which demonstrates that PVDF has been decomposed at a pyrolysis temperature of 500 ^∘C. In the pyrolysis process, a part of the polymer structure o - (CH2 - CF2) - n decomposes to a single molecule of CH2 = CF2 while others separate out HF and their carbon chain fracture to form small molecules. Ethylene carbonate and propylene carbonate are from residual electrolyte. These results demonstrate that the main organics in electrode materials are organic binder and electrolyte and pyrolysis can effectively remove organic binder and electrolyte.

Effects of Pyrolysis on the Physicochemical Properties of Electrode Materials. After the crushing and sieving processes, phase compositions of the raw electrode materials and pyrolytic electrode materials with a size of −0.075 mm were tested by XRD, and their results were shown in Figure 5. No new material peaks are detected by XRD in LiCoO or graphite, which indicates that crystal structures of LiCoO2 or graphite are not changed at a pyrolysis temperature of 500 ^∘C. At a pyrolysis temperature of 5̇ 00 ^∘C, only decomposition of organic binders happens on the surface of the electrode material particles, and it does not influence the physicochem ical properties of electrode materials; this is an advantage for the subsequent separation process. XRD results demonstrate that 500 ^∘ not only can remove organic binders but also does not change the properties of electrode materials

Changes in Surface Properties of Electrode Particles by Pyrolysis. Surface chemical compositions of raw LiCoO2 and pyrolytic LiCoO2 were analyzed by XPS. XPS wide energy spectra of LiCoO2 before and after pyrolysis are shown in

(b) Graphite

Chemical states of surface elements of raw LiCoO2 and pyrolytic LiCoO2 were carefully analyzed using XPS, and the C 1s spectra of raw LiCoO2 and pyrolytic LiCoO2 particles were shown in Figure 7 and Table 1. The C 1s spectrum of raw LiCoO2 particles presents a peak at 284.22 eV which is caused by the addition of carbon black, and its atomic percentage is 36.73%. Two main peaks of - (CH2CF2) - n and -̅ (CH2 C̅F2) - n that are attributed to PVDF were observed at 286.05 and 290.30 eV, respectively, and their atomic percentage is 19.03% and 5.18% in raw LiCoO2 particles, which indicates the organic binder still remains on the surfaces of the electrode powders. Peaks presented at 287.14, 288.06, and 289.00 eV are related to O - C - O, C = O, and _ O - C = O which are from ester electrolyte, such as ethylene carbonate and propylene carbonate. After pyrolysis, peaks of - (CH2CF2) - n and - (CH2CF2) - n derived from PVDF and C = O and O - C = O derived from electrolyte have been removed, but at the same time, four new peaks are found on the surface of pyrolytic LiCoO2 particles; they are pyrolytic carbon, C F, C - C F in trifluorobenzene, and _ C - C F in trifluorobenzene, which indicates that a part of the pyrolysis products and residue remain on the surface of the LiCoO2 particles. The main existing form of C on the surface of LiCoO2 particles is pyrolytic carbon, and its content is up to 63.50 %. The decrease of oxygen-containing functional groups on the surfaces of electrode particles is advantageous for the flotation of LiCoO2 and graphite, but the residue of pyrolytic carbon may be a disadvantage for the flotation; therefore, the ultrasonic cleaning process is utilized to remove residual pyrolytic products on the surface of pyrolytic electrode particles.

Surface Morphology Analysis of LiCoo2 and Graphite before and after Pyrolysis. Surface morphology analysis of raw LiCoO2 and graphite with −0.075 mm size derived from

spent LIBs was conducted by SEM, and the SEM images are shown in Figure 8. Because the organic binders have not been removed in the crushing process of the electrode materials, the agglomeration still exists in raw LiCoO2 and graphite particles. In addition, the individual particles that have detached from each other also comprise some organic binders on their surfaces. The SEM images present electrode particles have rough surfaces because of the residual organic binders. Surface morphology analysis indicates two main reason that raw LiCoO2 and graphite are hard to be separated by flotation: (1) Electrode particles are cladded by organic binders to form agglomeration that decrease the hydrophilic differences between LiCoO2 and graphite. (2) The individual particles also comprise some organic binder, and their surfaces are rough; this increases the hydrophilicity of graphite. SEM analysis demonstrates that removing organic binders is an essential process in the recycling process of spent LIBs.

Surface morphology analysis of pyrolytic LiCoO2 and graphite with - 0.075 mm size derived from spent LIBs also conducted by SEM, and the SEM images are shown in Figure 9. From the SEM images, we can find that the agglomeration of electrode materials has disappeared and they have been adequately detached from each other. Organic binders have been removed, and a smooth surface is present after pyrolysis. However, there are some residual pyrolysis products on the surface of the pyrolytic electrode particles, and their main contents are pyrolytic carbon with strong hydrophobicity. Therefore, some pyrolytic LiCoO2 particles may easily attach to a bubble and are collected in a frothy product, which result in a low recovery of LiCoO2. To improve the recovery rate, the residual pyrolysis products should be removed.

Flotation Test of LiCoo2 and Graphite with Different Pretreatment. Flotation experiments of electrode materials (REM, PEM, PUEM) with - 0.075 mm size were conducted to separate graphite and LiCoO2. The flotation results are given in Table 2 and Figure 11. The LiCoO2 grade in REML i o O2 concentrate is only 67.25% with the recovery of 74.62%. The LiCoO2 grade in PEM LiCoO2 concentrate is up to 94.00% with the recovery of 84.61% whereas it is up to 93.89% in PUEM LiCoO2 concentrate with the high recovery of 96.88%. The high recovery rate of LiCoO2 in REM is caused by the high yield of REM LiCoO2 concentrate with large amounts of graphite remaining. After pyrolysis pretreatment, the organic binder and electrolyte have been removed and the LiCoO2 grade in PEM LiCoO2 concentrate increases to 94.00 %. However, the residual pyrolysis products comprising hydro phobic properties remain on the surface of pyrolytic LiCoO2 particles, and some LiCoO2 particles also attach to bubbles and mix with frothy products; this is the main reason that a low recovery of 84.61% is obtained. The flotation result of PUEM demonstrates that ultrasonic cleaning can assist flotation behavior because the pyrolysis residues have been removed. This research demonstrated that flotation is a useful process to recover LiCoO2 from an electrode materials mixture, and the pyrolysis-ultrasonic pretreatment can improve the recovery efficiency of LiCoO2

Mechanism of Flotation Enhancement of LiCoo2 and Graphite by Pyrolysis−Ultrasound. Surface properties and morphology of raw LiCoO2 and graphite indicate that the existence of residual electrolyte and organic binder result in the hard flotation process of LiCoO2 and graphite. A schematic diagram of LiCoO2 and graphite particles with different pretreatments is shown in Figure 12. LiCoO2 and graphite particles are cladded by organic binder with strong hydrophobicity, and they cannot attach on the bubbles; this results in the low LiCoO2 grade in LiCoO2 concentrate. Pyrolysis can make organic binder and electrolyte fully decompose, but some pyrolytic carbon remains on the surface of pyrolytic LiCoO2 and graphite particles. Both LiCoO2 and graphite particles will attach on the bubbles. This results in some LiCoO2 particles mixing with the frothy products, which is the main reason that a low recovery of LiCoO2 in PEM is obtained. Ultrasonic cleaning is used to remove the residual pyrolysis products; the original surfaces of LiCoO2 and graphite are exposed, so LiCoO2 particles are hydrophilic while graphite is hydrophobic. The graphite particles will attach on the bubble’s surface while LiCoO2 remains in the pulp. Therefore, pyrolysis-ultrasonic flotation can be used to achieve high flotation separation of LiCoO and graphite.

## ■ CONCLUSION

Pyrolysis-ultrasonic-assisted flotation for recovering LiCoO2 and graphite from a spent lithium-ion battery has been fully studied. Mineralogical characteristics indicate that organic binder, residual electrolyte, and rough surfaces result in the hard flotation process of LiCoO2 and graphite. Basic pyrolysis characteristics of LiCoO2 and graphite indicate that organic binders can be decomposed thoroughly under a pyrolysis temperature of 500 ^∘C, and the main pyrolysis products are fluorine-containing benzene and ester electrolyte. SEM and XPS analyses indicate that some residual pyrolysis products remain on the surface of electrode material particles, and ultrasonic cleaning can remove them and effectively strengthen flotation behavior. The LiCoO2 grade improved from 67.25% to 93.89% while its recovery improved from 74.62% to 96.88% by pyrolysis-ultrasonic-assisted flotation. Parameter optimization experiments should be conducted in further research works to recover much purer electrode materials. This research work may provide an alternative environmentally-friendly flowchart to recycle LiCoO2 and graphite from spent LIBs.

records.section_name: ■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Pyrolysis Characteristics of Electrode Materials. Pyrolysis characteristics of raw LiCoO and graphite derived from spent LIBs are analyzed by TG-GC/MS. The TG results are shown in Figure 3, and pyrolysis products at pyrolysis temperatures of 120 and 500 ^∘ that correspond to the weight loss peaks in the DTG curve are present in Figure 4. The first weight loss stage appears when pyrolysis temperature ranges from 30 to 150 ^∘C; this is mainly caused by the volatilization of residual electrolyte. The decomposition of organic binder causes the second weight loss during the temperature of 450 to 550 ^∘C.. Similar TG and DTG curves of LiCoO2 and graphite demonstrate that the LiCoO2 and graphite used in this study have the same organic binder of PVDF. The DTG analysis shows the maximum weight loss appears at 500 ^∘C, and it indicates that pyrolysis can make organic binders fully decompose at 500 ^∘Ċ. source_evidence.quote: Sample Pyrolysis Procedures. First, pyrolysis characteristics of cathode and anode materials were, respectively, analyzed by TG-GC/ MS which included a thermogravimetric analyzer (TGA) (Labsys Evo1600, France), auto injector system (Automation Autoinjector Corp., Italy), and GC/MS (TRACE GC Ultra/ISQ Single Quadrupole MS, USA). TG tests were first conducted to analyze the decomposition process of organics in raw LiCoO and graphite particles, and then, pyrolysis products at weight loss temperature were collected and injected into the GC/MS system by an auto injector system. Pyrolysis experiments of electrode material mixtures were conducted in a controlled atmosphere tube furnace (MXG1200-80, Shanghai Micro-X furnace Co., Ltd.). In each experiment, the 5 g sample was placed into the corundum tube and the tube was sealed by flanges at both ends. A vacuum pump was first applied to provide the vacuum environment, and then, the corundum tube was filled with high purity nitrogen with the gas flow of 200 mL/min. Gas pyrolysis products could be taken out of the tube by nitrogen flow, and then, macromolecular organics could be collected by condensation while small molecule organic gases were treated by a gas-treating system. Pyrolysis temperature increased from an initial temperature of ∴ _ 30 to a terminal temperature of 500 ^∘C at a heating rate of 10 ^∘C / m i n. Samples would be processed at an isothermal temperature of 500 °C for 30 min. Afterward, the samples were naturally cooled to 30 ^∘C in a nitrogen atmosphere. After pyrolysis, a part of the pyrolytic electrode material was treated by ultrasound at solid/liquid ratio of 1:10 g/mL with an ultrasonic frequency of 25 kHz and electric power of 800 W for 2 h. Afterward, electrode materials were separated by the filtration method and dried at 80 ^∘C. By these processes, three samples were prepared for flotation: raw electrode material mixture (REM), pyrolytic electrode material mixture (PEM), and pyrolysis-ultrasonic pretreated electrode material mixture (PUEM).

Pyrolysis Characteristics of Electrode Materials. Pyrolysis characteristics of raw LiCoO and graphite derived from spent LIBs are analyzed by TG-GC/MS. The TG results are shown in Figure 3, and pyrolysis products at pyrolysis temperatures of 120 and 500 ^∘ that correspond to the weight loss peaks in the DTG curve are present in Figure 4. The first weight loss stage appears when pyrolysis temperature ranges from 30 to 150 ^∘C; this is mainly caused by the volatilization of residual electrolyte. The decomposition of organic binder causes the second weight loss during the temperature of 450 to 550 ^∘C.. Similar TG and DTG curves of LiCoO2 and graphite demonstrate that the LiCoO2 and graphite used in this study have the same organic binder of PVDF. The DTG analysis shows the maximum weight loss appears at 500 ^∘C, and it indicates that pyrolysis can make organic binders fully decompose at 500 ^∘Ċ. Therefore, the pyrolysis experiments are conducted at a temperature of 500 ^∘C

On the basis of the TG analysis, the pyrolysis products of electrode materials at temperatures of 120 and 500 ^∘C were sampled via the auto injector system that was connected with the GC and TGA system, and gas analysis was conducted in the GC/MS system. Figure 4 demonstrates that pyrolysis products at a pyrolysis temperature of 120 ^∘C come from ester electrolyte, such as dimethyl carbonate, ethylene carbonate, and propylene carbonate. Organic pyrolysis products at a pyrolysis temperature of 500 ^∘C are mostly fluorides that mainly come from the decomposition of PVDF, such as vinylidene fluoride, 1,3,5-trifluorobenzene, 1,4-difluoroben zene, ^1, 1, 1, 3, 3, 3 -hexafluoro-propane, and 1,2,4-trifluoroben zene, which demonstrates that PVDF has been decomposed at a pyrolysis temperature of 500 ^∘C. In the pyrolysis process, a part of the polymer structure o - (CH2 - CF2) - n decomposes to a single molecule of CH2 = CF2 while others separate out HF and their carbon chain fracture to form small molecules. Ethylene carbonate and propylene carbonate are from residual electrolyte. These results demonstrate that the main organics in electrode materials are organic binder and electrolyte and pyrolysis can effectively remove organic binder and electrolyte.

In each experiment, the 5 g sample was placed into the corundum tube and the tube was sealed by flanges at both ends. A vacuum pump was first applied to provide the vacuum environment, and then, the corundum tube was filled with high purity nitrogen with the gas flow of 200 mL/min. Gas pyrolysis products could be taken out of the tube by nitrogen flow, and then, macromolecular organics could be collected by condensation while small molecule organic gases were treated by a gas-treating system. Pyrolysis temperature increased from an initial temperature of ∴ _ 30 to a terminal temperature of 500 ^∘C at a heating rate of 10 ^∘C / m i n. Samples would be processed at an isothermal temperature of 500 °C for 30 min. Afterward, the samples were naturally cooled to 30 ^∘C in a nitrogen atmosphere. After pyrolysis, a part of the pyrolytic electrode material was treated by ultrasound at solid/liquid ratio of 1:10 g/mL with an ultrasonic frequency of 25 kHz and electric power of 800 W for 2 h. Afterward, electrode materials were separated by the filtration method and dried at 80 ^∘C. The TG results are shown in Figure 3, and pyrolysis products at pyrolysis temperatures of 120 and 500 ^∘ that correspond to the weight loss peaks in the DTG curve are present in Figure 4. The first weight loss stage appears when pyrolysis temperature ranges from 30 to 150 ^∘C; this is mainly caused by the volatilization of residual electrolyte. The decomposition of organic binder causes the second weight loss during the temperature of 450 to 550 ^∘C.. Similar TG and DTG curves of LiCoO2 and graphite demonstrate that the LiCoO2 and graphite used in this study have the same organic binder of PVDF. The DTG analysis shows the maximum weight loss appears at 500 ^∘C, and it indicates that pyrolysis can make organic binders fully decompose at 500 ^∘Ċ. Therefore, the pyrolysis experiments are conducted at a temperature of 500 ^∘C

On the basis of the TG analysis, the pyrolysis products of electrode materials at temperatures of 120 and 500 ^∘C were sampled via the auto injector system that was connected with the GC and TGA system, and gas analysis was conducted in the GC/MS system. Figure 4 demonstrates that pyrolysis products at a pyrolysis temperature of 120 ^∘C come from ester electrolyte, such as dimethyl carbonate, ethylene carbonate, and propylene carbonate. Organic pyrolysis products at a pyrolysis temperature of 500 ^∘C are mostly fluorides that mainly come from the decomposition of PVDF, such as vinylidene fluoride, 1,3,5-trifluorobenzene, 1,4-difluoroben zene, ^1, 1, 1, 3, 3, 3 -hexafluoro-propane, and 1,2,4-trifluoroben zene, which demonstrates that PVDF has been decomposed at a pyrolysis temperature of 500 ^∘C. In the pyrolysis process, a part of the polymer structure o - (CH2 - CF2) - n decomposes to a single molecule of CH2 = CF2 while others separate out HF and their carbon chain fracture to form small molecules. Ethylene carbonate and propylene carbonate are from residual electrolyte. These results demonstrate that the main organics in electrode materials are organic binder and electrolyte and pyrolysis can effectively remove organic binder and electrolyte.
